name: King's Gambit Declined
summary: The King's Gambit Declined (1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5) sidesteps the gambit pawn and develops the bishop to eye White's weakened kingside.
intro: The King's Gambit Declined arises after 1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5, when Black politely refuses the offered f-pawn and instead develops the bishop to c5. The bishop rakes the a7-g1 diagonal toward White's king, and by keeping the centre closed Black aims to punish the loosening of White's kingside rather than grab material.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: By declining the pawn with 2...Bc5, Black immediately trains the bishop on the a7-g1 diagonal, the very diagonal that 2.f4 has begun to expose. The key point is that White can no longer comfortably play fxe5 in many lines, because after ...d6 and the recapture the position simply opens toward the white king while Black keeps a healthy, mobile structure. Rather than defending an extra pawn as in the accepted lines, Black stakes everything on sound development and on the latent weakness of the e1-h4 and a7-g1 diagonals.

A recurring motif is the threat of ...Qh4+, which becomes available whenever White plays a careless f4-f5 or allows the f-file to open at the wrong moment; even without checks, the pressure on g1 restrains White's natural plans. White for his part would like to complete development with Nf3, c3 and d4, gaining central space and challenging the c5-bishop, but the knight on f3 must permanently watch the h4-square. The resulting middlegames are less chaotic than the accepted gambit, revolving instead around whether White's central pawns become an asset or the f4-advance a lasting liability.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The main line runs 3.Nf3, developing and covering h4, after which 3...d6 supports e5 and prepares to meet fxe5 with a comfortable recapture. White frequently continues with 4.c3, intending d4 to gain the centre and hit the c5-bishop, while Black completes development with ...Nf6, ...Nc6 and ...O-O, keeping an eye on the f4-pawn. A sharper independent try is 3.Nc3, when 3...Nf6 leads to positions related to the Vienna Game, and the fianchetto-style 4.fxe5 or 4.d3 setups give the play its own character.

The most combative alternative for White is 3.Nf3 d6 4.b4, the Rosentreter-flavoured gambit thrust that attacks the c5-bishop and grabs queenside space; Black usually retreats ...Bb6 and continues developing. Black can also meet the whole system with the immediate ...Nf6 and ...Nc6 setups, and White sometimes tries the aggressive f4-f5 clamp when circumstances allow. Throughout, the theoretical burden is lighter than in the King's Gambit Accepted, and both sides rely more on understanding the diagonal battle than on memorised forcing lines.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The King's Gambit Declined, and 2...Bc5 in particular, has been known since the earliest analyses of the King's Gambit in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, offered as a sober answer to a famously aggressive opening. It was a practical favourite among players who respected the gambit's dangers but preferred not to enter the wildest accepted lines, and it retained a following through the romantic era and into modern club play. Its reputation is that of a solid, slightly underrated response: Black concedes nothing material yet keeps genuine chances to exploit the kingside weaknesses that 2.f4 inevitably creates.

keyIdeas: Black declines the f-pawn and plays 2...Bc5 to pressure the a7-g1 diagonal.
Keeping the centre closed lets Black exploit White's loosened kingside.
The ...Qh4+ resource lurks whenever White's kingside opens carelessly.
White seeks c3 and d4 to gain the centre and challenge the c5-bishop.
The Nf3-knight must permanently guard the h4-square.
Lighter theory than the Accepted, decided by the diagonal battle.

white: Develop with Nf3 first to cover h4 before undertaking anything else.
Prepare c3 and d4 to build a broad centre and hit the c5-bishop.
Consider the b4 thrust to gain space and harass the dark-squared bishop.
Avoid premature fxe5 or f5 that would open lines toward the white king.
Complete development and castle before committing the central pawns.
black: Post the bishop on c5 and support the e5-pawn with ...d6.
Keep the ...Qh4+ idea in reserve to punish kingside carelessness.
Complete development with ...Nf6, ...Nc6 and short castling.
Retreat the bishop to b6 if challenged by c3-d4 or b4, keeping the diagonal.
Aim counterplay at the f4-pawn and the weakened e1-h4 diagonal.
